name: HotpotQA
summary: 7,405 questions that each need two Wikipedia paragraphs to answer, given with ten paragraphs to read and the sentences a person used to reach the answer.
overview:
HotpotQA asks questions that cannot be answered from any single paragraph. Each question was written by a crowdworker who was shown two Wikipedia paragraphs at once and asked for something that requires both, so answering means finding a fact in one paragraph and using it to reach the other. The workers also marked the sentences they had used, which the dataset publishes as supporting facts, making it one of the few question-answering datasets where a model's reasoning can be scored and not just its answer. It was built by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, Stanford University, and Université de Montréal, and published at EMNLP 2018 with 112,779 questions. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.09600)

The paragraph pairs were chosen to make genuine two-step questions. For bridge questions the authors followed a hyperlink from one article's opening paragraph to another, so the first paragraph names the entity the second is about; for comparison questions they drew two articles from one of 42 curated lists of similar entities, which yields questions that set two things side by side and often want a yes or no. Workers were also asked which sentences the answer depended on, and the authors held back the questions a single-paragraph model could already answer, keeping only the hard ones for evaluation. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.09600)

The benchmark is evaluated in two settings. In the distractor setting, which this snapshot holds, a model reads the two paragraphs the question was written from plus eight paragraphs retrieved for the same question as plausible decoys, all shuffled together, so it has to tell the relevant pair from the rest. In the fullwiki setting it must find the paragraphs itself among the first paragraphs of over five million articles. The authors' own baseline reached 44.44 answer exact match and 58.28 answer F1 on this split, with 11.56 joint exact match once supporting facts were counted too, while the crowdworkers they measured against each other reached 83.60 answer exact match and 52.30 joint exact match. The best distractor-setting submission on the leaderboard, Beam Retrieval from BUPT and Tencent in August 2023, reports 72.69 answer exact match, 85.04 answer F1, and 50.53 joint exact match on the hidden test set. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.09600) and [leaderboard](https://hotpotqa.github.io/)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete official development split in the distractor setting, the published file `hotpot_dev_distractor_v1.json`: 7,405 questions, all of them from the dataset's hard portion, of which 5,918 are bridge questions and 1,487 are comparisons. The training split of 90,447 questions, the same development questions in the fullwiki setting, where the ten paragraphs are retrieved rather than given, and the unlabelled fullwiki test split are not imported. The authors' download host no longer resolves, so the file is read from the Internet Archive's copy of their download link and pinned by its SHA-256 digest; a copy published on Hugging Face by the authors' organisation holds the same 7,405 rows. [Snapshot of the official download link](https://web.archive.org/web/20260310132809id_/http://curtis.ml.cmu.edu/datasets/hotpot/hotpot_dev_distractor_v1.json)

Each Task Prompt is the question followed by its paragraphs, each introduced by a heading naming the article it opens. The paragraphs appear in the shuffled order upstream records, so nothing marks which two the question was written from. They are the opening paragraphs of English Wikipedia articles as of the dump of 1 October 2017, stored upstream as lists of sentences and written back here as paragraphs; the sentence boundaries, which Stanford CoreNLP produced, are what the supporting-fact annotation points at. 7,345 questions come with ten paragraphs and the remaining 60 with between two and nine. A paragraph averages 4.2 sentences and 550 characters, and the longest runs to 85 sentences. Across the split the paragraphs come from 66,581 distinct articles.

The Solution is the answer, then the supporting facts. 225 answers are yes and 233 are no, which comparison questions invite; the other 6,947 are short text answers, and all but four of those appear verbatim in the paragraphs given with the question. Each supporting fact is written as the article title, the sentence number as upstream records it counting from zero, and that sentence: 4,990 questions have two, 1,774 have three, 537 have four, and 104 have between five and eight, and in every question they come from exactly two articles, the pair the question was written from. One supporting fact names sentence 902 of a five-sentence paragraph, an upstream annotation error that is kept as recorded with no sentence text beside it. Keys are the upstream question identifiers.

Every article is credited. HotpotQA records the title of each paragraph's article but not the revision it came from, so the ATTRIBUTION.md the importer regenerates lists all 66,581 articles with links to them, and each prompt names the article its paragraphs open. Prompt and solution links point at the pinned split file, which has no per-question addresses. The importer uses only Python's standard library, refuses the file if its digest differs, checks that every supporting fact names a paragraph that is present, and can be rerun with python3 data/hotpotqa/import.py.
scoring:
The official script scores a prediction with three pairs of numbers. For the answer it reports exact match and token F1 after lowercasing, removing punctuation and the articles a, an, and the, and collapsing whitespace, with the extra rule that a prediction of yes or no scores zero unless the reference is that same word. For the supporting facts it compares the predicted set of article and sentence-number pairs with the annotated set, reporting exact match, which requires the sets to be identical, and F1 over them. The joint numbers combine the two: joint precision and recall are the products of the answer and supporting-fact precisions and recalls, joint F1 is their harmonic mean, and joint exact match is 1 only when both the answer and the supporting-fact set are exactly right. Every number is averaged over the questions. [Evaluation script](https://github.com/hotpotqa/hotpot/blob/master/hotpot_evaluate_v1.py)

Because supporting facts are scored as a set of sentence addresses, a model has to name the sentences it used in the dataset's own numbering, which is why the joint numbers sit so far below the answer numbers: the authors' baseline scored 58.28 answer F1 but 40.86 joint F1 on this split. Official test numbers come from submitting a model to the leaderboard, which runs it on a hidden test split; numbers computed on this development split are self-reported, and the distractor and fullwiki settings are reported separately and are not comparable. [Project page](https://hotpotqa.github.io/)

Benchopedia stores the questions, the paragraphs, the answers, and the supporting facts. It does not run the evaluation script or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
A question built from a hyperlinked pair of paragraphs is not always a question that needs two hops. In the authors' own analysis of 100 sampled evaluation questions, 6% could be answered from a single paragraph and 2% were not answerable at all, and a later study built a single-hop model, which reads one paragraph at a time and cannot combine two, that reached 67 answer F1, comparable with the multi-hop models of the time; in the same study people shown only part of the evidence still answered over 80% of the questions. Four answers in this split do not appear anywhere in the ten paragraphs given with their question. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.09600) and [single-hop analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02900)

The eight distractor paragraphs were retrieved by bigram tf-idf against the question, so they are decoys of a particular kind: lexically similar openings about other entities. A model that learns which paragraphs look retrieved rather than chosen is reading the construction of the task, not the question. Scoring the supporting facts as sentence addresses also rewards matching one worker's judgement of which sentences mattered; a correct answer justified by a different sentence loses supporting-fact credit, and the single annotation per question means there is no measure of how much annotators would have disagreed.

The paragraphs are only the opening paragraph of each article, from a 2017 dump, with the hyperlinks stripped and the sentence boundaries fixed by a tokeniser of the period. Nothing in a prompt points at the live article, 66,581 articles have had nine years of editing since, and no revision is recorded, so a reader checking the encyclopedia today may find a different paragraph. One supporting fact points at a sentence that does not exist, which no prediction can match.

The split has been public since 2018, is widely used as training data for retrieval and reading models, and carries no canary string, so a model may have seen these questions, paragraphs, and answers in training; only the hidden test split offers a measurement free of that doubt.
